props.title: Late Spring
props.initialSlug: A daughter resists marriage to stay with her father

sections.content: Late Spring (1949) represents Yasujirō Ozu at his most masterful, using his signature "tatami-level" camera position and contemplative pacing to explore the changing dynamics of post-war Japanese family life. The story of Noriko (Setsuko Hara) and her widowed father Professor Somiya (Chishū Ryū) captures the tension between traditional family obligations and modern independence. This film established what would become known as the "Noriko trilogy," continuing with Early Summer (1951) and Tokyo Story (1953), all starring Hara as different characters named Noriko navigating family expectations and personal autonomy.

sections.content: Ozu's influence resonates through contemporary Asian cinema, particularly in the work of Hirokazu Kore-eda. Still Walking (2008) and Our Little Sister (2015) echo Late Spring's careful examination of family bonds and obligations. The measured pace, careful composition, and focus on domestic spaces in Edward Yang's Yi Yi (2000) and Wong Kar-wai's In the Mood for Love (2000) also show clear debts to Ozu's aesthetic approach.

Late Spring's themes of generational conflict and familial duty have influenced filmmakers worldwide. Paul Schrader's First Reformed (2017) directly references Ozu's style, while Sofia Coppola's Lost in Translation (2003) explores similar themes of cultural obligation and personal desire in modern Japan. The film's exploration of parent-child relationships can be traced through works like The Farewell (2019) and Shoplifters (2018). SUBHEAD: Post-War Japanese Society and Family

sections.content: Late Spring emerged during a crucial period of Japanese history, as traditional values clashed with American occupation and modernization. This context influenced a wave of Japanese films including Akira Kurosawa's Drunken Angel (1948) and Mikio Naruse's Mother (1952). Ozu's approach to these social changes was uniquely subtle, focusing on the quiet devastation of necessary separation rather than dramatic conflict.
